title: No blaming
hook: let no one hear you blame court life, not even yourself (Meditations 8.9)

segments.voice: Yesterday: look at the thing, the carpenter's eyes on the wood. Your line was steadily. Which task did you look straight at? Day five hundred ninety-eight.

Listen to any break room, any family group chat, any line at the post office. This place is a mess. My boss doesn't get it. The traffic in this city. My job is killing me. Complaining can be friendly. It's how strangers bond in a stalled elevator. And it can quietly take over a whole life. Marcus Aurelius had an emperor's share of things to complain about. In book eight he wrote himself a rule about it, in a single sentence.
screen: `THE BREAK ROOM CHORUS.` → `FRIENDLY, AND CORROSIVE.` → `A ONE-LINE RULE.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. Meditations eight, nine, says: let no one hear you any longer finding fault with life at court, or with your own life. That's all. One sentence. Second, the court. Remember Marcus's stepmother picture from book six: the court as the stepmother, philosophy as the mother. The court was where the flattery was, the scheming, the endless petitions. He had every reason to grumble. And he tells himself to stop, at least out loud. Third, the second half. Notice he adds, or with your own life. Complaints about the world are one habit. Complaints about yourself are another. I'm hopeless. I always mess this up. Marcus closes both. Not because things are perfect. Because complaining, in either direction, doesn't change the next action, and it trains the mind to see only the faults. Fourth, what it isn't. This isn't a ban on naming real problems. The rule is about finding fault, not about fixing things. A plan to fix something isn't a complaint. Telling a friend you're struggling isn't either. The target is the background hum of blame, the grumbling that goes nowhere. Try listening for it for one day, and it can be startling how much of ordinary talk it fills. Marcus's rule is simple: catch it, and stop. Even mid-sentence. Then turn back to what you can actually do.
screen: `NO FAULT-FINDING, OUT LOUD.` · `THE COURT, HIS STEPMOTHER.` · `NOT WITH YOUR OWN LIFE EITHER.` · `A PLAN IS NOT A COMPLAINT.` · then, large: `NO BLAMING.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind your most familiar complaint. About work, a person, the city, yourself. Hear it in your own voice. Now, gently, let it stop halfway. Let the sentence just hang. Notice the quiet after it. In that quiet, ask: is there one thing I can actually do about this? If there is, picture it. If there isn't, just breathe. The bell holds the time.
No blaming. Marcus's one-line rule: let no one hear you find fault with your circumstances, or with your own life. Today's word.
Your line: no blaming. Today, catch one complaint mid-sentence, stop it, and turn it into one thing you can do, or into silence. Day five hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus sometimes keep a no-complaining rule, catching grumbles about their circumstances or themselves and turning them into a plan or letting them go.
